Third. On several occasions, in authorizing blending of 
adulterated with unadulterated corn, the FDA has made 
statements indicating that action levels establish a binding form.
* * * [I]n a formal notice published in the Federal Register of a 
decision to permit blending and interstate shipment, FDA wrote:
Any food that contains aflatoxin in excess of 20 ppb ... is 
considered by FDA to he adulterated under section 402(a)(1) 
of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 
342(a)(1)), and therefore may not he shipped in interstate 
commerce.
46 Fed.Reg. 7447 (1981) (emphasis added). * * * The agency’s own 
words strongly suggest that action levels are not musings about 
what the FDA might do in the future but rather that they set a 
precise level of aflatoxin contamination that FDA has presently 
deemed permissible. Action levels inform food producers what this 
level is; indeed, that is their very purpose.
Id. at 947-48.
The court in Cmty. Nutrition Inst, faced a somewhat perplexing 
problem. The action levels did not harm regulated parties (on the contrary, 
they gave regulated parties a safe harbor), but there was a serious concern 
that the action levels, by being too lax, harmed people who might consume 
adulterated food and would therefore benefit from stronger regulation 
(known as “regulatory beneficiaries”). If the agency adhered to its guidance, 
it would enforce only if the thresholds were exceeded (thresholds the 
activists befieved so high as to undermine public health), and the 
enforcement proceedings would afford no opportunity for regulatory 
beneficiaries to challenge the agency’s policies. On the other hand, if 
agencies do not intend to abide by their policy statements, they are of little 
use in controlling lower level personnel or informing the affected pubhc. 
And if “practically binding on the agenc/’ is the test for whether guidance 
is really a legislative rule, the APA exception for policy statements may be 
narrow indeed. This and other conundra have haunted the application of 
the Pacific Gas and Cmty. Nutrition Inst, principles, as the following case 
attests.
